**Answer: Yes.** The measure $\mu\{\omega : |f(\omega)| = \alpha\}$ is zero for all but countably many real numbers $\alpha$.

**Proof.**

Set $g = |f| \geq 0$, and for each $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ define the level set
$$A_\alpha := \{\omega \in \Omega : g(\omega) = \alpha\}.$$
Since $g \geq 0$, we have $A_\alpha = \emptyset$ (hence $\mu(A_\alpha)=0$) for every $\alpha < 0$. So it suffices to consider $\alpha \geq 0$.

The key observation is that the family $\{A_\alpha\}_{\alpha \geq 0}$ is **pairwise disjoint**: if $\alpha \neq \beta$, a point $\omega$ cannot simultaneously satisfy $g(\omega)=\alpha$ and $g(\omega)=\beta$.

Define the set of "bad" levels
$$S := \{\alpha \geq 0 : \mu(A_\alpha) > 0\}.$$
We claim $S$ is countable. For each integer $n \geq 1$, set
$$S_n := \left\{\alpha \geq 0 : \mu(A_\alpha) \geq \tfrac{1}{n}\right\}.$$
Then $S = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} S_n$ (since any positive real number exceeds $1/n$ for some $n$).

Now fix $n$. The sets $\{A_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in S_n}$ are pairwise disjoint, each with measure $\geq 1/n$, and all contained in $\Omega$ which has total measure $\mu(\Omega)=1$. If $S_n$ contained $n+1$ distinct elements $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_{n+1}$, then by disjointness
$$\mu\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n+1} A_{\alpha_i}\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} \mu(A_{\alpha_i}) \geq \frac{n+1}{n} > 1 = \mu(\Omega),$$
a contradiction. Hence $|S_n| \leq n$; in particular $S_n$ is **finite**.

Therefore
$$S = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} S_n$$
is a countable union of finite sets, hence **countable**.

For every $\alpha \notin S$ (and there are all but countably many such $\alpha$), we have $\mu(A_\alpha) = 0$, i.e.,
$$\mu\{\omega : |f(\omega)| = \alpha\} = 0.$$

**Remark.** The integrability of $f$ was not actually needed; measurability of $f$ alone suffices. The only ingredients are measurability of $g=|f|$ (giving measurable level sets) and the finiteness of $\mu(\Omega)=1$ (giving the bound on how many disjoint sets of positive measure can coexist). $\blacksquare$
